title: The Prophets Stir, the King Agrees
sum: In the second year of Darius, 520 BC, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urge the Jews of Judea and Jerusalem to build, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin work on the Lord's house. Sisinnes, the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, comes to ask who allowed it. The elders are not stopped, "because the Lord had come to watch over the captives," and the governor writes to Darius. His letter quotes the elders' answer: they serve the Lord who made heaven and earth, their ancestors' sins brought the first house down, and Cyrus ordered it rebuilt and gave the vessels to Zerubbabel and Sanabassar.

Darius has the archives searched, and Cyrus's memo turns up at Ecbatana in Media. Darius then orders the governor to keep away, to let Zerubbabel, "the Lord's servant," build, and to pay for the sacrifices out of the province's taxes, so that prayers may be offered for the king. Anyone who breaks the decree is to be hanged and his property seized. The chapter follows Ezra 5:1-6:12 closely, but adds Zerubbabel's name in three places where Ezra has none.
readings: Most historians accept that the temple was rebuilt under Darius I between 520 and 515 BC, as Haggai, Zechariah and Ezra say, and that Persian kings supported local temples. Whether the letters are copies of real Persian documents is debated; in 1 Esdras they are also clothed in Greek letter forms and Greek-era place names, so this book is a step further from the archive than Ezra.

In 1 Esdras, Darius has just promised Zerubbabel, the winner of the guards' contest, that the temple will be built (4:42-57). This chapter shows the promise kept: the vessels are "given to Zerubbabel," Darius names him "the Lord's servant," and the allowance is paid "to Zerubbabel the governor." The narrator of Ezra keeps Zerubbabel in the background; 1 Esdras puts him at the center.

views.O: Orthodox readers have this chapter twice in their Old Testament, here and in Ezra 5-6, and can read the two side by side. Read together, both say that God moves kings to rebuild his house, and that the prophets' word comes first: building begins when Haggai and Zechariah speak.
views.H: Critical scholars note the Greek-era names (Syria and Phoenicia, Coele-Syria) and the Greek letter opening, and use them to date the translation. They also discuss the tension in 6:17-19, where Zerubbabel receives the vessels but only Sanabassar lays the foundation, as a sign that 1 Esdras has added Zerubbabel to an older story.
views.J: Josephus retells these events with Zerubbabel prominent, as 1 Esdras does. Ezra 5-6 is part of the Jewish Bible; 1 Esdras is not, and later Jewish tradition knows the rebuilding from Ezra, Haggai and Zechariah.
views.S: Beside Ezra 5:1-6:12: the date moves to 6:1; Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai become Sisinnes and Sathrabuzanes; "Beyond the River" becomes Syria and Phoenicia; the officials ask both questions (no puzzling "we," Ezra 5:4); "great" describes the house, not God (6:8); the God of the heavens and the earth becomes the creator (6:12); the burning is added (6:15); the vessels go to Zerubbabel as well as Sanabassar (6:17); the sacrifices burn with continual fire (6:23); Zerubbabel is named in Darius's order (6:26, 6:28); the penalty is hanging and confiscation, not impaling and a dunghill (6:31).
views.W: Western readers have usually met these events in Ezra 5-6. The Anglican Article VI lists 1 Esdras, under its Latin name "the Third Book of Esdras," among books the church reads "for example of life" but does not use "to establish any doctrine," and the Council of Trent's list of Scripture names only the first and second books of Esdras (Ezra and Nehemiah). So for Western churches the Ezra form of this chapter is Scripture, and this one is a witness to how it was read.

deep.b: Ezra 1:8 and 5:14-16 credit Sheshbazzar with bringing the vessels and laying the foundation; Ezra 3:8-10, Haggai and Zechariah credit Zerubbabel with the building. Readers have long asked whether they were one man with two names or two men. 1 Esdras answers in its own way by naming both: the vessels go "to Zerubbabel and to Sanabassar the governor" (6:17), and then Sanabassar lays the foundation (6:19). The verses that follow speak of one man, which suggests Zerubbabel's name was added to a sentence about Sheshbazzar alone. See the topic pages on Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel.

deep.title: Claude's reading: a decree that answers the guards' contest
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. In 4:42-57 Zerubbabel asks Darius to keep the vow made at his accession to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple, and Darius writes letters on his behalf. Chapter 6 then gives the Ezra form of the same permission, with Zerubbabel written in. Read in this order, the search of the archives (6:20-25) confirms what the king had already granted for Zerubbabel's wisdom, so the story has two foundations for the temple: the king's favor to a wise Jew, and the old decree of Cyrus. The book may intend the reader to see God working through both.

settings.what: The prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah
settings.by: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
settings.to: The Jews in Judea and Jerusalem, and their leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua
settings.when: In the second year of Darius, 520 BC, after years in which the building had stood still
settings.why: To move the people to build the Lord's house now. 1 Esdras gives no words of theirs; the books of Haggai and Zechariah do.
settings.readers: The Greek of 1 Esdras uses names and titles of the Greek period (Coele-Syria, Friends of the king, philanthropa), so most scholars date the translation to the 200s or 100s BC and think of Greek-speaking Jews, in Egypt or in Judea, as its first readers; where exactly is debated. The earliest reader we can name is Josephus, who followed this book in Antiquities 11 at the end of the first century AD.

settings.by: Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, with Sathrabuzanes and their colleagues
settings.to: The Jewish builders and their elders
settings.why: To find out whether the building had royal permission, the first duty of a provincial governor. The question is not hostile in itself; it sets up the search that will confirm the right to build.

settings.by: Sisinnes and Sathrabuzanes and their colleagues
settings.why: To report the work, pass on the elders' claim that Cyrus had ordered it, and ask the king to search the archives and rule. The letter quotes the elders' own account (6:12-19), so the Jews' history is told to the king in their words.

settings.to: Sisinnes and his colleagues, and through their letter, the king
settings.why: To explain who they are (servants of the creator), why the first house fell (their ancestors' sin), and by what right they build (Cyrus's decree). It is a short confession of Israel's history for a foreign ruler.

settings.by: Cyrus, as recorded in the scroll at Ecbatana
settings.why: To authorize the rebuilding of the house, set its size, pay its cost, and return the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken.

settings.to: Sisinnes and the officials of Syria and Phoenicia, and through them the Jews
settings.why: To protect the building, fund the sacrifices from provincial taxes, gain prayers for the king and his sons, and threaten anyone who interferes. In 1 Esdras it also honors Zerubbabel by name.
views: A real Persian decree in Greek dress
Some historians think the Ezra form goes back to a genuine Persian document, which 1 Esdras renders freely with Greek-era terms.
Others think the letters were composed by Jewish writers to show Persian support, and 1 Esdras develops them further.

title: The House Finished and the Passover Kept
sum: The governors obey Darius and oversee the work with the Jewish elders, and the temple is finished on the twenty-third of Adar in Darius's sixth year, early in 515 BC. It is dedicated with a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs and twelve goats for the twelve tribes, and the priests and Levites take their places "according to the book of Moses."

On the fourteenth of the first month the returned exiles keep the Passover, after the priests and Levites have been purified, and they keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because God turned the heart of "the king of Assyria" toward them. The short chapter follows Ezra 6:13-22 and closes the first half of the book's story: the house destroyed in chapter 1 stands again.
readings: 1 Esdras begins with Josiah's great Passover (1:1-20) and here reaches another Passover in the rebuilt house. The book moves from a Passover before the fall to a Passover after the return, as if to show that worship has been restored where it broke off.
Read as Ezra's chapter in Greek
Most of the chapter matches Ezra 6:13-22. The changes are small but telling: no joy at the dedication, the book of Moses moved forward, and no room for outsiders at the Passover (7:13).

views.O: For Orthodox readers, who have both Ezra 6 and this chapter in their Old Testament, the two accounts tell the same story: the rebuilt house is crowned by the Passover, the feast of the Exodus that the church reads in the light of Christ's Pascha.
views.H: Historians take the completion date in 515 BC as reliable in substance; the twenty-third of Adar in 1 Esdras and the third in Ezra cannot both be right. Critical scholars also note that the chapter's focus on purity and the separated community prepares for the marriage reform of chapters 8-9.
views.J: In Jewish history the Second Temple, finished here, stood until AD 70. Ezra 6 is read as Scripture in Judaism; 1 Esdras survived in Christian copies of the Greek Bible.
views.S: Beside Ezra 6:13-22: the officials work with the elders and "temple overseers" (7:2); the consent of the kings, not their command (7:4); the twenty-third of Adar (7:5); no joy at the dedication (7:6); priests and Levites by "tribes," with gatekeepers added (7:9); a doubled purification clause (7:10-11); the Passover eaters are only the separated exiles, without Ezra's outsiders who join them (7:13).
views.W: Western churches read this account in Ezra 6, which they hold as Scripture; 1 Esdras is printed in the Apocrypha of some Protestant Bibles and in the appendix of the Clementine Vulgate.

deep.b: The law allowed a foreigner living among Israel to keep the Passover once circumcised (Exodus 12:48). Ezra 6:21 seems to allow it too: the exiles ate "along with everyone who had separated himself to them from the uncleanness of the nations of the land." 1 Esdras 7:13 reads the same words so that the separated ones are the exiles themselves. Whether this is a different Hebrew text or the translator's reading, it makes the community a closed group, which fits the strict demand of 8:65-9:36. Readers of both books can compare Isaiah 56:3-7, where foreigners who hold to the covenant are welcome in God's house.

title: Ezra Comes, and the News He Hears
sum: Some sixty years later, under Artaxerxes, Ezra comes from Babylon: a priest of Aaron's line, gifted in Moses' law, who leaves out nothing of it. The king's letter lets any Jews, priests and Levites who wish go with him, sends gifts for the temple, gives him money from the treasuries of Syria and Phoenicia, frees the temple staff from taxes, and makes him judge and teacher of the law for the Jews of the province. Ezra blesses the Lord and gathers the families who will go up.

At the river he finds no priests or Levites and sends for them; he proclaims a fast instead of asking the king for soldiers, and he entrusts the treasure to twelve priests. The company reaches Jerusalem safely and offers sacrifices. Then the leaders report that priests, Levites and nobles have married women of the foreign peoples. Ezra tears his clothes and sits in grief until the evening sacrifice, then kneels and confesses the people's sins (8:71-87). A large crowd gathers weeping, and Jechonias proposes an oath to send away the foreign wives and their children. The chapter follows Ezra 7:1-10:5, in Greek.
readings: Read as a portrait of Ezra

1 Esdras makes Ezra larger than life: gifted, learned, a priest in a "holy robe," the king's favorite and the "reader" of the law. The Hebrew Ezra is also a great figure, but 1 Esdras, which has no Nehemiah, gives him the whole stage.

The center of the chapter is the prayer of 8:71-87. A leader who has not sinned himself confesses "our sins," and the people answer with weeping and a promise. Read this way, the chapter is about repentance, and the marriage question is its occasion.

views.O: Ezra's prayer stands beside the prayers of Daniel 9 and Nehemiah 9 as a model of confession. Because 1 Esdras is in the Orthodox Old Testament, its Greek form, with its "errors" and its "root and name" (8:72, 8:75), is part of the text Orthodox readers have alongside the Ezra form.
views.H: Historians debate whether Ezra came in 458 BC (Artaxerxes I) or 398 BC (Artaxerxes II), and whether the letter of 8:9-24 is a real Persian document. The Greek of 1 Esdras is no help on the date, since it has no Nehemiah to compare. Its Hellenistic terms (philanthropa, Friends, Syria and Phoenicia) show that the translator presented the letter in the language of the royal charters of his own day.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers Ezra as a second Moses. A teaching in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 21b) says, in the name of Rabbi Yosei, that Ezra was worthy for the Torah to be given through him had Moses not come first, setting "This Ezra went up from Babylon" (Ezra 7:6) beside Moses going up to God (Exodus 19:3). Josephus tells Ezra's journey and the marriage reform in the order of 1 Esdras, with Jechonias as the man who proposes the oath (Antiquities 11.145).
views.S: Beside Ezra 7:1-10:5: three generations missing in Ezra's line (8:2); "gifted" and "great knowledge" for Ezra's heart set on the law (8:3, 8:7); "reader of the law" for "scribe" (8:8); the king's letter in Hellenistic terms, with "Syria and Phoenicia" for "Beyond the River"; worn-down names and some different numbers in the list (8:29-40); "the River" and Thera for Ahava; no priests as well as no Levites (8:42); Casiphia translated "the Treasury" (8:44); a fast "for the young men" (8:49); goats as a peace offering, not a sin offering (8:63); Edomites in the list of peoples (8:66); "lawlessness" for "unfaithfulness" (8:67); "errors" for "guilt" (8:72); "true" for "in the right" (8:86); an oath, not a covenant (8:90).
views.W: Western readers know this story from Ezra 7-10. The Anglican Article VI lists 1 Esdras as "the Third Book of Esdras" among books read "for example of life," and Ezra's prayer is the kind of example that phrase has in mind; but the church "doth not apply them to establish any doctrine."

deep.b: The Hebrew calls Ezra a sofer, "scribe." 1 Esdras uses that word once (8:3) and then, five times, anagnōstēs, "reader" (8:8, 8:9, 8:19; 9:39, 9:42, 9:49). The title prepares for the last scene, where Ezra reads the law aloud to all the people. It also fits the readers of the Greek book: Jews who heard Scripture read in Greek, and for whom the public reader was a familiar figure.

Ezra's prayer (8:71-87) follows Ezra 9:6-15 verse by verse, but its images change. The Hebrew "tent peg" and "band of survivors" become "a root and a name"; the "fence" becomes "a firm footing"; "guilt" becomes "errors," sins done unknowingly; and the LORD who is "in the right" becomes the Lord who is "true." The Greek prayer leans toward hope: God has left a root, and his faithfulness is the reason the people are still alive.

deep.title: Claude's reading: why "errors"?
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not a published view I have checked. 1 Esdras uses agnoia, "error, ignorance," in Ezra's prayer (8:72) and again for the priests' rams (9:20), where the Hebrew speaks of guilt. In the law a ram atones for a sin done without knowing (Leviticus 5:18). If the translator saw the marriages as sins of ignorance, the order of the book makes sense: the people sin without knowing the law, confess, put the sin right, and then hear the whole law read so that they will know it (9:37-55). The book would then end where it means to, with a people who now know.

echoes: Ezra 7:1-10:5; Nehemiah 9:6-37; Daniel 9:4-19; Deuteronomy 7:1-6; Leviticus 18:24-30; Isaiah 6:13; Malachi 2:10-16

settings.to: Ezra the priest and reader, and through him the treasurers of Syria and Phoenicia and the Jews of the province
settings.when: In the king's seventh year, before Ezra leaves Babylon
settings.why: To give Ezra a royal charter: leave for any Jews to go with him, gifts and funds for the temple, tax freedom for its staff, and power to appoint judges and teach the law. For the first readers it presented the law of Moses as backed by royal authority, in the language of Hellenistic royal grants.
settings.readers: The Greek of 1 Esdras uses names and titles of the Greek period (Coele-Syria, Friends of the king, philanthropa), so most scholars date the translation to the 200s or 100s BC and think of Greek-speaking Jews, in Egypt or in Judea, as its first readers; where exactly is debated. The earliest reader we can name is Josephus, who followed this book in Antiquities 11 at the end of the first century AD.
views: Some scholars think the letter in Ezra 7:12-26 is based on a genuine Persian order, which 1 Esdras renders freely.
Others think it was written to show that the law and the temple had royal support.

settings.by: Ezra (in Vaticanus the speaker is not named; see the note)
settings.to: God, in the hearing of the book's readers
settings.why: To give the credit for the king's favor to the Lord, and to explain Ezra's courage in gathering men to go up.

settings.to: God, with the people who were traveling
settings.when: Before the dangerous journey from Babylon to Jerusalem
settings.why: To ask God for a safe road, since Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him and was ashamed to ask for soldiers.

settings.to: The twelve chief priests and their companions entrusted with the gifts
settings.why: To remind them that they and the gifts are holy to the LORD, and to make them answerable for every item until it is weighed out in the temple.

settings.when: After his arrival and the sacrifices
settings.why: To tell him that the rulers, priests and Levites had married women of the foreign peoples, so that "the holy seed" was mixed with them.

settings.to: God, in the hearing of those gathered at the temple
settings.when: At the evening sacrifice, after a day of grief
settings.why: To confess the people's sins as his own, to recall God's mercy in leaving them a root, and to admit that they cannot stand before him. Its public setting makes it also a sermon: the crowd that gathers responds with weeping and a plan.
settings.readers: The Greek of 1 Esdras uses names and titles of the Greek period (Coele-Syria, Friends of the king, philanthropa), so most scholars date the translation to the 200s or 100s BC and think of Greek-speaking Jews, in Egypt or in Judea, as its first readers; where exactly is debated. The earliest reader we can name is Josephus, who followed this book in Antiquities 11 at the end of the first century AD.

settings.when: While Ezra lies weeping before the temple
settings.why: To confess the sin and propose an oath to send away the foreign wives and their children, and to urge Ezra to lead it. The plan comes from the people, not from Ezra.

title: The Marriages Undone and the Law Read
sum: Ezra spends the night fasting in a temple room, and a call goes out for all the exiles to come to Jerusalem within two or three days or lose their livestock to the temple. They gather on the twentieth of the ninth month, shivering in the winter rain, and agree to Ezra's demand but ask for time and for local courts. Leaders sit from the first of the tenth month to the first of the first month, and a list follows of priests, Levites and laymen who had married foreign wives, ending: "they sent them away with their children" (9:36).

Then, on the first day of the seventh month, the people gather before the temple's east gate, and Ezra, "the high priest and reader," reads the law from dawn until noon from a wooden platform, with men beside him and Levites teaching the people. The people weep; Attarates, Ezra and the Levites tell them that the day is holy, that they must eat, share with the poor and rejoice, "because the LORD will give you glory." The people go off to feast, because the words had breathed life into them. "And they gathered together." There the book stops.
readings: On this reading the last words open a scene that has been lost, likely the Feast of Booths as in Nehemiah 8:13-18 and Josephus. The book would once have gone on, perhaps to Ezra's death, and the ending we have is an accident of the manuscripts.

On this reading the book was meant to end with the people gathered around the law. It began with Josiah's Passover and the book of the law found in his day (2 Chronicles 34-35), and it ends with the law read to all the people; temple, Passover and law have all been restored.

views.O: For Orthodox readers the reading of the law has a familiar shape: a priest on a raised platform, the book lifted up, the people standing, the "Amen," and Levites who teach. The Greek word for the platform, bema, is the word for the sanctuary of an Orthodox church.
views.H: Critical scholars discuss two questions. First, the order: the Hebrew puts the reading in Nehemiah 8, 1 Esdras after Ezra 10, and some think 1 Esdras keeps an older order of the Ezra story while others think it gathered Ezra's scenes together. Second, the ending: most think the book is broken off, since its last clause starts something new, and note that Josephus goes on to the Feast of Tabernacles and Ezra's death (Antiquities 11.154-158).
views.J: In Jewish tradition Ezra's reading is the model for the public reading of the Torah, and the Talmud remembers his days as the time when the Torah was given again in the square "Ashurit" script (Sanhedrin 21b). The raised bimah of the synagogue takes its name from the Greek bema of 9:42. Josephus tells the reading straight after the divorces, as 1 Esdras does, and sets it at the Feast of Tabernacles (Antiquities 11.154-157).
views.S: Beside Ezra 10:6-44 and Nehemiah 7:73-8:12: Ezra spends the night (9:2); two or three days, and the livestock "consecrated" (9:4); winter (9:6); the four men help rather than oppose (9:14); different and worn-down names in the list; the wives and children are sent away (9:36); the reading follows at once, at the temple's east gate rather than the Water Gate (9:38); Ezra is "high priest" and "reader" (9:40); seven and six men beside him (9:43-44); Azarias blesses God (9:46); the Levites "breathe life into" the reading (9:48); no Nehemiah, but Attarates (9:49); "the LORD will give you glory" (9:52); the book ends at Nehemiah 8:12-13.
views.W: Western readers know these scenes from Ezra 10 and Nehemiah 8. In the Clementine Vulgate this book stands in the appendix after the New Testament as 3 Esdras, outside the books the Council of Trent listed; Article VI lists it among the books read for example of life.

deep.b:
The Greek ends with kai episynēchthēsan, "and they were gathered together." In Nehemiah 8:13 the next sentence begins the same way: the family heads "gathered to Ezra the scribe" the next day, and the Feast of Booths follows. So the Greek seems to stop at the first words of the next scene.

Evidence for a lost ending. The last clause starts a new action, and the book has no closing formula. Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras rather than Ezra-Nehemiah in his order of events, goes on: the people keep the Feast of Tabernacles for eight days in booths, and Ezra dies an old man and is buried "in a magnificent manner at Jerusalem" (Antiquities 11.157-158). He may have had a longer copy, or he may have added these things from Nehemiah 8 and tradition.

Evidence for a planned ending. The book also begins abruptly, with Josiah's Passover (1:1), and seems to be cut from a longer history at both ends. Some readers see a frame: a feast at the start, a feast at the end, and the law at the center of both (1:1-20; 9:37-55). The KJV reads the last words as part of the sentence before and so ends with a complete sentence: "for the which they had been assembled."

The Plain translates what the Greek has, a full stop after "they gathered together," and leaves the question open.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the breath of the law
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The verb emphysioō, "breathe into," is used twice at the end of the book: the Levites "breathe life into" the reading (9:48), and the words "breathe life into" the people (9:55). The related verb is used when God breathes life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and into the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). If the translator chose it on purpose, the book ends with a new creation: a people who were "a root" left in the ground (8:86) are given breath by the law. That would make "And they gathered together" a fitting last line, like the bones that "came together" in Ezekiel 37:7.

echoes: Ezra 10:6-44; Nehemiah 7:73-8:18; Deuteronomy 31:9-13; 2 Kings 23:1-3; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Malachi 2:10-16; Luke 4:16-21

settings.by: The leaders and elders, in Ezra's name
settings.to: All the people of the exile in Judea and Jerusalem
settings.why: To bring every man to Jerusalem within two or three days, under threat of losing his livestock and his place in the community.

settings.to: The men of Judah and Benjamin, sitting in the temple court in the winter rain
settings.when: The twentieth of the ninth month
settings.why: To name the sin, call for confession and praise to God, and demand separation from the foreign wives.
settings.readers: The Greek of 1 Esdras uses names and titles of the Greek period (Coele-Syria, Friends of the king, philanthropa), so most scholars date the translation to the 200s or 100s BC and think of Greek-speaking Jews, in Egypt or in Judea, as its first readers; where exactly is debated. The earliest reader we can name is Josephus, who followed this book in Antiquities 11 at the end of the first century AD.

settings.why: To agree, and to ask for a workable plan: time, local elders and judges, and an end to God's anger.

settings.by: Ezra, with Levites who teach and read
settings.to: All the people, men and women, and all the priests, in the square before the temple's east gate
settings.when: The first day of the seventh month, from dawn to noon
settings.why: To put the law of Moses before the whole community in a public act, so that they hear it, understand it and live by it. In 1 Esdras it comes right after the marriage reform, as if to give the people the knowledge whose lack had led them into sin.
settings.readers: The Greek of 1 Esdras uses names and titles of the Greek period (Coele-Syria, Friends of the king, philanthropa), so most scholars date the translation to the 200s or 100s BC and think of Greek-speaking Jews, in Egypt or in Judea, as its first readers; where exactly is debated. The earliest reader we can name is Josephus, who followed this book in Antiquities 11 at the end of the first century AD.
views: Some scholars think the reading once followed Ezra 10, as here.
Others think 1 Esdras or its source brought the reading here from its place in Nehemiah.

settings.by: Attarates (the governor's title read as a name), and the Levites
settings.to: Ezra and all the weeping people
settings.when: As the people weep at hearing the law
settings.why: To turn grief into celebration: the day is holy, so the people must eat, share with the poor and rejoice, trusting that the Lord will give them glory.
